module_6.m6_cells_need_energy: p86: cells need energy for work: movement, growth, pumping ions, running reactions
module_6.m6_phototroph_chemotroph: p86: phototrophs get energy from sunlight; chemotrophs from chemical compounds
module_6.m6_autotroph_heterotroph: p86: autotrophs make organic carbon from CO2; heterotrophs must take in organic carbon
module_6.m6_metabolic_pathways_linked: p87: metabolism is linked reactions: the product of one reaction is the reactant of the next
module_6.m6_anabolism_catabolism: p87: anabolism builds molecules and needs energy (ATP); catabolism breaks them down and releases energy
module_6.m6_potential_kinetic: p87: potential energy is stored, kinetic energy is motion; energy converts between forms
module_6.m6_bond_energy: p88: chemical energy is potential energy in bonds; strong bonds hold less potential energy than weak bonds
module_6.m6_atp_structure: p88: ATP = adenine + ribose + three phosphates; ADP has two, AMP one
module_6.m6_atp_currency: p88: ATP stores energy in an accessible form that all cells use for cellular work
module_6.m6_first_law: p89: energy is neither created nor destroyed, only converted from one form to another
module_6.m6_second_law: p89: energy transformations are not 100% efficient; some energy is lost as heat, raising entropy
module_6.m6_reaction_direction_concentration: p90: in a reaction atoms keep their identity while bonds change; concentrations of reactants and products affect direction
module_6.m6_delta_g_sign: p90: exergonic reactions (negative delta G) are spontaneous and release energy; endergonic ones (positive delta G) need an input
module_6.m6_gibbs_equation: p91: delta G = delta H - T delta S
module_6.m6_atp_hydrolysis_exergonic: p91: ATP hydrolysis is exergonic (-7.3 kcal/mol) because the negative phosphates repel
module_6.m6_activation_energy: p91: every reaction needs activation energy; reactants need enough kinetic energy to cross the barrier
module_6.m6_enzymes_lower_ea: p91: enzymes speed reactions by lowering activation energy; delta G is unchanged
module_6.m6_driving_positive_dg: p92: cells run positive-delta-G reactions by keeping concentrations away from equilibrium or by coupling
module_6.m6_energetic_coupling: p92: coupling an endergonic reaction to ATP hydrolysis through a shared intermediate gives a negative net delta G
module_6.m6_active_site: p92: the active site forms when folding brings distant amino acids together; it binds substrate and stabilizes the transition state
module_6.m6_induced_fit: p93: lock-and-key vs induced fit: the enzyme changes shape when substrate binds
module_6.m6_enzyme_cycle: p93: E + S -> ES -> EP -> E + P; the enzyme is released unchanged and reused
module_6.m6_competitive_inhibition: p93: a competitive inhibitor binds the active site; extra substrate overcomes it
module_6.m6_noncompetitive_inhibition: p93: a noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme's shape; extra substrate does not overcome it
module_6.m6_reversible_irreversible: p93: inhibitors are reversible (bind and leave) or irreversible (permanently inactivate the enzyme)
module_6.m6_enzyme_activators: p93: activators bind an enzyme and increase its activity
module_6.m6_feedback_inhibition: p93: the end product of a pathway inhibits its first enzyme (allosteric enzyme), saving energy and materials

module_7.m7_respiration_fuels: p96: cellular respiration can use carbohydrates, lipids and proteins and converts their energy into ATP
module_7.m7_four_stages_order: p96: the four stages in order: glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation
module_7.m7_stage_locations: p101: glycolysis happens in the cytosol; stages 2-4 happen in the mitochondria
module_7.m7_substrate_level: p97: substrate-level phosphorylation makes a small amount of ATP directly in an enzyme reaction
module_7.m7_oxphos_most_atp: p97: most ATP is made by oxidative phosphorylation, powered by electrons the carriers deliver to the ETC
module_7.m7_redox_definitions: p97: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain; the two always occur together
module_7.m7_glucose_oxidized_o2_reduced: p97: in respiration glucose is oxidized to CO2 and O2 is reduced to H2O
module_7.m7_carriers_nad_fad: p98: NAD+ and FAD are the oxidized carriers; NADH and FADH2 are the reduced, high-energy forms
module_7.m7_stepwise_energy_release: p98: glucose's free energy is released step by step and stored as ATP and reduced carriers
module_7.m7_glycolysis_overview: p99: glycolysis: ten reactions split six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvates in the cytosol
module_7.m7_glycolysis_no_o2: p99: glycolysis consumes no O2 and runs with or without it
module_7.m7_glycolysis_phase1: p100: phase 1 (preparatory) spends 2 ATP to make fructose 1,6-bisphosphate
module_7.m7_phosphorylation_traps_glucose: p100: phosphorylating glucose traps it in the cell and destabilizes it for splitting
module_7.m7_glycolysis_phase2: p100: phase 2 cleaves fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into G3P and DHAP; DHAP becomes a second G3P
module_7.m7_glycolysis_phase3: p101: phase 3 (payoff) makes 4 ATP, 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate from 2 G3P
module_7.m7_glycolysis_net_yield: p101: glycolysis nets 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose
module_7.m7_mito_compartments: p102: mitochondria have an outer and inner membrane, an intermembrane space and a matrix
module_7.m7_pyruvate_oxidation_step: p102: in the matrix, pyruvate is oxidized to CO2 and an acetyl group, which joins coenzyme A; NADH forms (pyruvate dehydrogenase complex)
module_7.m7_pyruvate_oxidation_totals: p103: per glucose, pyruvate oxidation gives 2 CO2, 2 NADH and 2 acetyl-CoA
module_7.m7_cac_cycle_regenerates: p103: the citric acid cycle is a cycle because oxaloacetate, which accepts acetyl-CoA, is regenerated
module_7.m7_cac_completes_oxidation: p103: the citric acid cycle completes the oxidation of the fuel; its carbons leave as CO2
module_7.m7_cac_yield: p106: per glucose the cycle makes 6 NADH, 2 FADH2 and 2 ATP (as GTP), plus 4 CO2
module_7.m7_cac_intermediates_biosynthesis: p103: cycle intermediates such as alpha-ketoglutarate feed other pathways (amino acids, purines)
module_7.m7_exhaled_co2: p104: the CO2 we exhale comes from pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle
module_7.m7_etc_location_components: p105: the ETC sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane: complexes I-IV, coenzyme Q and cytochrome c
module_7.m7_o2_final_acceptor: p105: O2 is the final electron acceptor and is reduced to water
module_7.m7_fadh2_enters_complex_ii: p105: NADH gives electrons to complex I; FADH2 gives them to complex II, bypassing complex I
module_7.m7_proton_pumping: p105: electron flow through complexes I, III and IV pumps protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space
module_7.m7_proton_gradient: p105: the gradient (high H+ in the intermembrane space, low in the matrix) stores potential energy because H+ cannot cross the membrane
module_7.m7_atp_synthase: p106: protons flow down their gradient through ATP synthase: the Fo channel rotates and F1 uses the rotation to make ATP
module_7.m7_chemiosmotic_coupling: p106: the proton gradient couples electron transport to ATP synthesis
module_7.m7_atp_yield_total: p106: complete oxidation of glucose yields about 32 ATP: 2 glycolysis, 2 cycle, about 28 oxidative phosphorylation
module_7.m7_fermentation_purpose: p107: without O2, fermentation regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can keep making ATP
module_7.m7_lactic_acid_fermentation: p107: in animal cells and bacteria pyruvate is reduced to lactic acid; no CO2 is released
module_7.m7_ethanol_fermentation: p107: in plants and fungi pyruvate releases CO2 to form acetaldehyde, which NADH reduces to ethanol
module_7.m7_fermentation_yield: p107: fermentation yields only glycolysis's 2 ATP per glucose, far less than aerobic respiration
module_7.m7_glycogen_starch_storage: p108: animals store glucose as glycogen, plants as starch; glucose units are released one at a time into glycolysis
module_7.m7_liver_vs_muscle_glycogen: p108: muscle glycogen powers that muscle's contraction; liver glycogen supplies the whole body
module_7.m7_other_sugars_enter: p108: dietary disaccharides and monosaccharides yield glucose or other glycolysis intermediates
module_7.m7_lipids_energy_rich: p109: lipids are excellent fuels because they are rich in C-C and C-H bonds
module_7.m7_beta_oxidation: p109: beta-oxidation cuts fatty acids into acetyl-CoA, making NADH and FADH2 but no ATP directly; glycerol enters glycolysis
module_7.m7_proteins_as_fuel: p109: proteins are broken into amino acids that can enter respiration at several points

module_8.m8_photosynthesis_definition: p112: photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy, building carbohydrate from CO2; it is life's main energy entry point
module_8.m8_photosynthesis_efficiency: p112: at most about 4% of incoming sunlight ends up stored in carbohydrate; much of it is outside the usable range, reflected or lost
module_8.m8_light_limits_habitat: p112: photosynthesis needs light, so in the ocean it happens only in the upper sunlit layer, which supports food webs
module_8.m8_photosynthesis_redox: p112: photosynthesis is a redox process: CO2 is reduced to carbohydrate and water is oxidized
module_8.m8_water_electron_donor: p112: water is the electron donor; oxidizing it releases electrons, protons and O2 as a by-product
module_8.m8_two_stages_linked: p112: light capture makes ATP and NADPH, which carbon fixation (Calvin cycle) uses
module_8.m8_chloroplast_structure: p113: chloroplasts have two membranes, thylakoids (stacked in grana), a thylakoid lumen and the surrounding stroma
module_8.m8_stage_locations: p113: light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes; the Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma
module_8.m8_overall_equation: p113: 6 CO2 + 12 H2O + light -> C6H12O6 + 6 O2 + 6 H2O
module_8.m8_photon_excitation: p113: absorbing a photon raises a pigment to an excited state
module_8.m8_excited_state_fates: p113: an excited pigment returns to ground state by heat, fluorescence (longer wavelength) or energy transfer
module_8.m8_spectrum_wavelength_energy: p114: visible light is 400-700 nm; shorter wavelengths carry more energy per photon
module_8.m8_chlorophyll_absorption: p114: chlorophyll absorbs blue and red light and absorbs green poorly, so leaves look green
module_8.m8_chlorophyll_structure: p114: chlorophyll's porphyrin ring (Mg at its centre) absorbs light; its hydrocarbon (phytol) tail anchors it in the thylakoid membrane
module_8.m8_accessory_pigments: p114: accessory pigments such as carotenoids absorb wavelengths chlorophyll misses and protect against damage
module_8.m8_antenna_transfer: p115: antenna chlorophylls pass absorbed energy (not electrons) to the reaction center
module_8.m8_reaction_center: p115: the reaction-center chlorophyll pair transfers an excited electron to an acceptor and must then get an electron from a donor
module_8.m8_two_photosystems_series: p116: photosystem II and photosystem I act in series, linked by the photosynthetic electron transport chain
module_8.m8_psii_water: p116: photosystem II takes the electrons it loses from water
module_8.m8_psi_nadph: p116: a second light input at photosystem I raises electrons high enough to reduce NADP+ to NADPH
module_8.m8_z_scheme: p116: the electrons' energy rises at PSII, falls along the chain, rises again at PSI: the Z scheme
module_8.m8_carriers_pq_pc: p117: plastoquinone carries electrons from PSII to the cytochrome b6f complex; plastocyanin carries them through the lumen to PSI
module_8.m8_thylakoid_proton_gradient: p117: electron flow moves H+ from the stroma into the lumen, so H+ is high in the lumen
module_8.m8_photophosphorylation: p117: H+ flowing from the lumen through thylakoid ATP synthase makes ATP on the stroma side (photophosphorylation)
module_8.m8_chloroplast_atp_stays: p117: chloroplast ATP stays in the chloroplast for carbon fixation, so plant cells also need mitochondria
module_8.m8_cyclic_electron_transport: p120 (term; textbook): in cyclic electron transport, electrons from PSI return to the cytochrome b6f complex, making ATP without NADPH or O2
module_8.m8_calvin_overview: p118: the Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH to turn low-energy CO2 into carbohydrate in three steps: carboxylation, reduction, regeneration
module_8.m8_carboxylation_rubisco: p119: rubisco adds CO2 to five-carbon RuBP; the six-carbon product splits into two 3-phosphoglycerate (PGA)
module_8.m8_reduction_step: p119: PGA is phosphorylated by ATP to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, which NADPH reduces to triose phosphate
module_8.m8_regeneration_rubp: p119: of every 6 triose phosphates, 5 are rearranged (using ATP) into 3 RuBP and only 1 leaves the cycle
module_8.m8_calvin_stoichiometry: p119: 3 CO2 fixed gives 1 net triose phosphate; per 3 CO2 the cycle uses 9 ATP and 6 NADPH
module_8.m8_starch_for_night: p119: excess carbohydrate is stored as starch by day and used at night

earlier_modules.m1_endosymbiosis: Module 1/3: mitochondria (from proteobacteria) and chloroplasts (from cyanobacteria) arose by endosymbiosis
earlier_modules.m1_prokaryote_no_organelles: Module 1: prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles, so their respiration chain sits in the plasma membrane
earlier_modules.m2_electronegativity_redox: Module 2: electronegativity: oxygen pulls electrons strongly, so electrons moving toward O release energy
earlier_modules.m2_nucleotide_structure: Module 2: nucleotides are base + sugar + phosphate; NAD+, FAD and ATP are nucleotide-based
earlier_modules.m2_polysaccharides_storage: Module 2: starch and glycogen are branched glucose polymers built by glycosidic bonds; cellulose is structural
earlier_modules.m2_condensation_hydrolysis: Module 2: condensation joins monomers releasing water; hydrolysis splits them using water
earlier_modules.m2_lipid_structure: Module 2: a triacylglycerol is glycerol plus three fatty acids, rich in C-H bonds
earlier_modules.m2_ph_hydrogen_ions: Module 2: pH measures H+ concentration; one pH unit is a tenfold difference
earlier_modules.m2_protein_folding_bonds: Module 2: a protein's shape depends on weak bonds that heat or pH changes disrupt
earlier_modules.m3_membrane_permeability: Module 3: the lipid bilayer blocks ions such as H+; they cross only through proteins
earlier_modules.m3_mito_chloro_membranes: Module 3: mitochondria and chloroplasts are double-membrane organelles with their own compartments
earlier_modules.m3_primary_active_transport: Module 3: primary active transport (pumps) uses energy to move ions against their gradient, building a gradient
earlier_modules.m3_secondary_active_transport: Module 3: secondary transporters use an existing ion gradient to move another solute
earlier_modules.m3_facilitated_diffusion_glut: Module 3: glucose enters cells down its gradient through GLUT carrier proteins
earlier_modules.m4_mtdna_genome: Module 4: mitochondria and chloroplasts carry their own small circular genomes
earlier_modules.m5_translation_ribosomes: Module 5: mitochondria have bacteria-like ribosomes; some antibiotics that target bacterial ribosomes also hit them
earlier_modules.m5_protein_targeting: Module 5: nuclear-encoded organelle proteins are made in the cytosol and imported using targeting signals
earlier_modules.m5_gene_mutation_protein: Module 5: a mutation in a gene can leave its enzyme missing or nonfunctional
